questions.q: Which of the following represents the number of elements in the dynamic array?
questions.explanation: `size` tracks how many elements are currently stored. `capacity` is the total allocated memory, and `arr` is the pointer to the underlying array buffer.

questions.q: Access time for the 10th element in a single-dimensional array is equal to....
questions.explanation: The general formula for element at logical index $i$ is $\text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times (i - \text{first\_index})$. Substituting $i = 10$ gives option (a).

questions.q: What is the access time required to retrieve the element located at position (5, 9) in a 7-row and 12-column array?
questions.explanation: Row-major formula (1-based indexing): $\text{addr}(r,c) = \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times ((r-1) \times n_{\text{cols}} + (c-1))$. With $n_{\text{cols}} = 12$, $r = 5$, $c = 9$: $\text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times ((5-1) \times 12 + (9-1))$.

questions.q: The complexity of adding three elements to the end of an array is.......
questions.explanation: Adding a constant number of elements is constant time overall. In Big O notation, constants are dropped: $O(3) = O(1)$.

questions.q: ............. have a constant-time access
questions.explanation: Arrays support $O(1)$ random access via index arithmetic: $\text{address} = \text{base} + \text{elem\_size} \times \text{index\_offset}$. No traversal is needed.

questions.q: What is the time complexity to find an element's position in a priority queue (LinkedList-based)?
questions.explanation: In a linked-list-based priority queue, finding an element requires traversing nodes one at a time. In the worst case every node is visited: $O(n)$.

questions.q: Which of the following operations is used to set the value of an element at index $i$ in a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: `Set(i, val)` writes a value at the given index, equivalent to `arr[i] = val`. `Get(i)` reads, `PushBack` appends, and `insert(i)` adds at a position.

questions.q: What happens if the tail variable is already pointing to a node when the PushFront(key) function is executed?
questions.explanation: PushFront inserts at the head. The last node (and therefore `tail`) does not change, so the tail variable is left unchanged.
options: The tail variable is updated to point to the new node
The tail variable is not updated
The tail variable is set to None
The tail variable is deleted from memory

questions.q: AddAfter(Node, Key) in a single linked list with a tail is .....
questions.explanation: Given a direct reference to the node, only pointer adjustments are needed — no traversal. If the node is the tail, `tail` is updated to the new node. Either way: $O(1)$.

questions.q: TopBack() in a single linked list with a tail is .....
questions.explanation: With a `tail` pointer, the last element is directly accessible in $O(1)$ — no traversal required.

questions.q: PushBack(Key) in a single linked list without a tail is .....
questions.explanation: Without a tail pointer, we must walk from `head` to the last node before appending. This traversal is $O(n)$.

questions.q: To return and remove the most recently added key in a stack, we use the ....... function
questions.explanation: `Pop()` removes **and** returns the top element (the most recently pushed key), implementing LIFO removal.

questions.q: Stack operation Push() is implemented using LinkedList ...... function
questions.explanation: A stack operates at one end only. Using a singly-linked list, `Push(key)` maps to `PushFront(key)` (inserts at head), so that `Pop()` = `PopFront()` retrieves the most recently added element in $O(1)$.

questions.q: What happens when the size of the dynamic array exceeds its capacity?
questions.explanation: When full, the dynamic array allocates a new larger buffer (typically double the capacity), copies all existing elements into it, and frees the old buffer.
options: A new, larger array is allocated, and the elements are copied over
The excess elements are automatically removed

questions.q: What is the overall time complexity of the Insert(e) operation in a priority queue (sorted array)?
questions.explanation: Binary search finds the insertion point in $O(\log n)$, but shifting all subsequent elements to make room takes $O(n)$. The dominant term gives an overall complexity of $O(n)$.

questions.q: In a dynamic array, when does the "index out of range" error message appear?
questions.explanation: Valid indices are $0$ to $\text{size} - 1$. An error occurs when the index is negative ($< 0$) **or** when it is $\geq \text{size}$ (beyond stored elements, even if within allocated capacity).
options: When the index provided is less than 0
When the index provided is greater than or equal to the capacity of the array
When the index is greater than or equal to the size of the array

questions.q: What is the best-case time complexity of Insertion Sort for an already sorted array?
questions.explanation: When the array is already sorted, Insertion Sort performs exactly $n - 1$ comparisons and zero swaps (each element is already in place), giving a best-case of $O(n)$.

questions.q: If tail = head, this means the linked list is empty?
questions.explanation: **False.** When `head == tail` and both are non-`nil`, the list contains exactly one node. The list is empty only when `head == nil` (and `tail == nil`). The condition `head == tail` alone does not imply empty.

questions.q: Find(Key) in a double linked list with a tail is .....
questions.explanation: Even with `prev` links and a tail pointer, finding an arbitrary key in an unsorted doubly-linked list still requires linear traversal in the worst case: $O(n)$.

questions.q: Erase(Key) in a single linked list with a tail is .....
questions.explanation: Erasing by key first requires finding the node (traversal = $O(n)$), then relinking the predecessor's `next` pointer. The traversal dominates: $O(n)$.

questions.q: Removes and returns the first added key from a Stack is known as ....
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO — only the **most recently** added element is accessible. Removing the *first* (oldest) element from a stack violates LIFO and is not a standard stack operation.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search?
questions.explanation: In the worst case (element absent or at the last position), Linear Search examines every element in the list: $O(n)$.

questions.q: Which algorithm is adaptive and performs well on partially sorted arrays?
questions.explanation: **Insertion Sort** is adaptive: its complexity degrades gracefully from $O(n)$ (fully sorted) to $O(n^2)$ (reverse sorted), making it efficient on nearly-sorted data. Binary Search is not a sorting algorithm.

questions.q: Which operation checks if the stack has elements?
questions.explanation: `Empty()` returns `true` when the stack contains no elements (e.g., `numElements == 0`), and `false` otherwise.

questions.q: When you apply PushBack in a Linked List containing one Node, you must update
questions.explanation: With one existing node, `head` already points to it and does not change. PushBack appends a new node at the end, so only `tail` must be updated to point to the new node.

questions.q: When apply pop() in Stack implemented with array you should
questions.explanation: Pop() removes the top element. In an array-based stack this is done by **decrementing** `numElements` (or the top index). No actual data deletion or resizing is required.

questions.q: ............. is indexed by contiguous integers.
questions.explanation: An **array** occupies a contiguous block of memory and is accessed using consecutive integer indices (0, 1, 2, …), enabling direct $O(1)$ index-based access.

questions.q: The access time for element (2, 4) in a 3-row and 6-column array is equal to.....
questions.explanation: Row-major formula (1-based): $\text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times ((r-1) \times n_{\text{cols}} + (c-1))$. For $(r,c) = (2,4)$ and $n_{\text{cols}} = 6$: $\text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times (1 \times 6 + 3) = \text{arr\_addr} + 9 \times \text{elem\_size}$.

questions.q: The complexity of adding two elements to the end of an array is.......
questions.explanation: Adding two elements is a constant-time operation. In Big O notation constants are dropped, so $O(2) = O(1)$.

questions.q: AddAfter(Node, Key) in a single linked list without a tail is .....
questions.explanation: When given a direct reference to the node, inserting after it requires only pointer adjustments — no traversal — regardless of whether a tail pointer exists: $O(1)$.

questions.q: Removes and returns the least recently-added key from a queue is known as ....
questions.explanation: `Dequeue()` removes and returns the **front** element (the least recently added key), implementing FIFO behavior.

questions.q: Stacks operations known as ........
questions.explanation: Stacks operate as **LIFO** (Last In, First Out). None of the given options match: FIFO describes queues, and LILO/MILO are not standard terms.

questions.q: PushBack(Key) in a single linked list with a tail is .....
questions.explanation: With a `tail` pointer, a new node is linked directly after `tail` and `tail` is updated — no traversal needed: $O(1)$.

questions.q: To return the most recently-added key in a stack, we use the ...... function
questions.explanation: `Top()` (or `KeyTop()`) **peeks** at the top element — the most recently pushed — and returns it without removing it.

questions.q: Queue operations are known as ........
questions.explanation: Queues operate as **FIFO** (First In, First Out): the first element enqueued is the first to be dequeued.

questions.q: In the Queue implementation with an array, if read = write + 1, we can perform Enqueue?
questions.explanation: **False.** In a circular array-based queue, `read = write + 1` (mod capacity) indicates the queue is **full** — the write index has wrapped around to the position just behind the read index. Enqueue would overwrite unread data.

questions.q: Appending a new element to a dynamic array is.......
questions.explanation: Appending is **amortized $O(1)$**: most appends are $O(1)$, and occasional resizes (copying $n$ elements) are amortized over many operations, keeping the average constant.

questions.q: The Function of adding an element to a stack is called
questions.explanation: `Push(key)` is the standard stack operation for adding an element to the top.

questions.q: Which of the following does not allow homogenous data elements?
questions.explanation: Arrays enforce a **homogeneous** structure — all elements must share the same type. A **LinkedList** can store heterogeneous data, since each node is independently allocated and can hold arbitrary data.

questions.q: An array of integers has `array_addr = 2000` and `first_index = 10`. What is the logical index $i$ for the element at physical address 2060?
questions.explanation:
Using the formula $\text{physical\_addr} = \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times (i - \text{first\_index})$ with `elem_size = 4` bytes (integer):
$$2060 = 2000 + 4 \times (i - 10) \implies 60 = 4(i-10) \implies i - 10 = 15 \implies i = 25$$

questions.q: What is the time complexity to access an arbitrary element in a full array containing $n$ elements?
questions.explanation: Array access uses direct index arithmetic (base address + offset), so any element is reached in constant time $O(1)$, regardless of $n$.

questions.q: In a 2D array with 6 columns (0-based index), what is the formula to find the offset for the element at row 3, column 4?
questions.explanation: With **0-based** indexing, the offset for element at row $r$, column $c$ with $n_{\text{cols}}$ columns is: $\text{elem\_size} \times (r \times n_{\text{cols}} + c) = \text{elem\_size} \times (3 \times 6 + 4) = 22 \times \text{elem\_size}$.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of removing an element from the beginning of an array?
questions.explanation: Removing from the beginning requires shifting all remaining $n - 1$ elements one position left to close the gap: $O(n)$.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of adding an element to the end of a full array?
questions.explanation: For a dynamic array, a full array triggers a resize: a new larger array is allocated and all $n$ existing elements are copied over — $O(n)$ in the worst case.

questions.q: In Array, which pair of operations both require $O(n)$ time?
questions.explanation: Both operations require shifting elements: **adding to the beginning** shifts all $n$ elements right ($O(n)$), and **removing from the middle** shifts all subsequent elements left ($O(n)$). Adding/removing from the end is $O(1)$.
options: Adding to the beginning and removing from the middle
Adding to the end and removing from the end
Adding to the middle and removing from the end
Removing from the beginning and adding to the end

questions.q: Why does PopBack() in a singly-linked list with a tail pointer NOT run in $O(1)$ time?
questions.explanation: After removing the last node, `tail` must point to the new last node. Since singly-linked nodes have no `prev` pointer, the only way to find the new tail is to traverse from `head`: $O(n)$.
options: Because the tail pointer must be securely deleted from memory.
Because finding the new tail requires traversing the list from the head.
Because the list must be completely copied to avoid memory leaks.
Because singly-linked lists do not allow backward traversal under any circumstances.

questions.q: In a singly-linked list, what is the time complexity of PushFront(Key)?
questions.explanation: PushFront creates a new node, sets its `next` to the current `head`, then updates `head` — all constant-time pointer operations: $O(1)$.

questions.q: When executing PopFront() on a singly-linked list, which operation updates the head?
questions.explanation: PopFront advances the head pointer to the next node: `head = head.next`. If the list becomes empty, `head` becomes `nil` and `tail` is also set to `nil`.

questions.q: In a singly-linked list, what is the time complexity of AddAfter(Node, Key)?
questions.explanation: Given a direct reference to the node, only two pointer assignments are needed to insert the new node — no traversal: $O(1)$.

questions.q: In a doubly-linked list WITH a tail pointer, what is the time complexity of PopBack()?
questions.explanation: With `tail` and `prev` pointers, the predecessor of the last node is accessed directly via `tail.prev`, and both `tail` and the new last node's `next` are updated in constant time: $O(1)$.

questions.q: If head == tail and head != nil, what is the state of the linked list?
questions.explanation: When `head` and `tail` point to the **same non-nil node**, the list contains exactly one element. Empty is when both are `nil`.

questions.q: How do you check if a singly linked list is "full"?
questions.explanation: Linked lists grow dynamically on the heap. There is no predetermined capacity — the list grows until memory is exhausted. Therefore, there is generally **no way** to check if it is "full".

questions.q: In a stack with array implementation, Empty() simply checks if
questions.explanation: An array-based stack tracks element count with `numElements`. `Empty()` simply returns `true` when `numElements == 0`.

questions.q: Which of the following operations takes $O(n)$ time in a typical stack implementation?
questions.explanation: All standard stack operations — Push, Pop, and Top — run in $O(1)$ time in both array-based and linked-list-based implementations. None takes $O(n)$.

questions.q: During AddAfter(node, key) in a doubly-linked list, node2.next is assigned to point to
questions.explanation: When inserting `node2` after `node`, `node2.next` must point to what was previously `node.next` (the successor), so the forward chain is preserved intact.

questions.q: Stack operations are known as
questions.explanation: Stacks follow **LIFO** (Last In, First Out): the most recently pushed element is the first to be popped.

questions.q: If an array-based stack holds elements [a, b, d, e] and Pop() is called, what is the updated sequence of elements left in the stack?
questions.explanation: Elements are pushed in order a → b → d → e, so `e` is at the top. Pop() removes the top element `e`, leaving [a, b, d].

questions.q: When implementing a Stack using a singly-linked list, we use:
questions.explanation: A stack only operates at one end. Using `PushFront` (insert at head) and `PopFront` (remove from head) gives $O(1)$ push and pop. Since the back is never accessed, no tail pointer is needed.

questions.q: What is the final state of the stack after Push(x), Push(y), Push(z), Pop(), Top(), Pop()?
questions.explanation:
Step-by-step:
- Push(x) → [x]
- Push(y) → [x, y]
- Push(z) → [x, y, z]
- Pop() → removes z → [x, y]
- Top() → peeks at y (no removal) → [x, y]
- Pop() → removes y → [x]

Final state: **x** remains.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of the Empty() operation in a full stack?
questions.explanation: `Empty()` checks a single condition (e.g., `numElements == 0`). This is always $O(1)$, regardless of how many elements are in the stack.

questions.q: In a linked list queue, how many pointers are changed during Dequeue()?
questions.explanation: Dequeue is implemented as `PopFront()`. The primary change is `head = head.next` (1 pointer). In the typical non-emptying case only 1 pointer changes. If the queue becomes empty, `tail` is also set to `nil` (2 pointers), but the standard answer is 1.

questions.q: In an array-based queue, what happens when the write index exceeds the array size and there are free locations available?
questions.explanation: Array-based queues use a **circular buffer**: when the write index reaches the end, it wraps around to index 0, reusing slots freed by Dequeue operations without resizing.

questions.q: In an array-based queue, the queue is empty when.......
questions.explanation: The queue is empty when `read == write` — the read pointer has caught up with the write pointer, meaning all previously enqueued elements have been dequeued.

questions.q: In a linked list queue, which method is used for Dequeue()?
questions.explanation: `Dequeue()` removes the front element of the queue, which corresponds directly to `PopFront()` on the linked list.

questions.q: Which term describes nodes sharing the same parent?
questions.explanation: **Siblings** are nodes that share the same parent in a tree structure. Ancestors are nodes above, descendants are nodes below, and leaves are nodes with no children.

questions.q: ....... is maximum depth of subtree node and farthest leaf
questions.explanation: The **height** of a tree (or subtree) is the length of the longest path from the root down to a leaf — the maximum depth among all leaves.

questions.q:
Which traversal visits nodes in the order:
Left subtree → Root → Right subtree
questions.explanation: **In-order traversal** follows the pattern Left → Root → Right. Applied to a Binary Search Tree, it visits nodes in ascending sorted order.

questions.q: ............. is a contiguous area of memory consisting of equal-size elements
questions.explanation: An **array** is defined as a contiguous block of memory where every element occupies the same fixed number of bytes, enabling $O(1)$ index-based access via arithmetic.

questions.q: The complexity of adding an element to the middle of an array is.......
questions.explanation: Inserting in the middle requires shifting all elements after the insertion point one position to the right to make room: $O(n)$ in the worst case.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT allow heterogeneous data elements?
questions.explanation: **Arrays** are homogeneous structures — every element must be of the same type. Linked lists allow heterogeneous nodes, and stacks/queues implemented with linked lists can also hold varied types.

questions.q: Each stack operation is ...
questions.explanation: All fundamental stack operations — Push, Pop, Top, and Empty — run in $O(1)$ time in both array-based and linked-list-based implementations.

questions.q: Find(Key) in a single linked list with a tail is ...
questions.explanation: Finding an arbitrary key requires scanning from `head` through the list. Even with a tail pointer, the worst case visits every node: $O(n)$.

questions.q: Erase(Key) in a single linked list with no tail is ...
questions.explanation: Erasing by key requires first finding the node (traversal = $O(n)$) and then relinking the predecessor. The traversal dominates: $O(n)$, regardless of the absence of a tail pointer.

questions.q: The dequeue operation is implemented using the ............ function:
questions.explanation: `Dequeue()` removes the front element of the queue — this maps directly to `PopFront()` on the underlying linked list. `TopFront()` only peeks without removing.

questions.q: In the Queue implementation with an array, the Queue is empty when ...
questions.explanation: The queue is empty when `read == write` — the read index has caught up with the write index, meaning no elements remain to be dequeued.

questions.q: When a dynamic array is full and a pushback operation is performed ...
questions.explanation: Dynamic arrays use a **doubling strategy**: when the array is full, the **capacity** is doubled (duplicated), a new larger buffer is allocated, and all elements are copied. This gives amortized $O(1)$ pushback.

questions.q: Enqueue is implemented using the ........ function
questions.explanation: `Enqueue()` adds a new element to the **back** of the queue, which corresponds to `PushBack(key)` on the underlying linked list.

questions.q: The drawback of dynamic arrays is that some space is wasted.
questions.explanation: **True.** The doubling strategy allocates more capacity than currently needed. At any point up to half of the allocated buffer may be unused, trading wasted space for amortized $O(1)$ appends.
